Lab 10: A Poll That Is Precise and Wrong

84-355 Democracy’s Data | Week 10

Your name here

August 05, 2026

Before we start

The country votes on Tuesday. Between now and then you will see a great many numbers with a ±3 attached to them, and it is worth knowing exactly what that number promises — and, more importantly, what it does not.

Every other lab this term handed you real data and asked what it showed. Today we do the opposite. We are going to build a population where we already know the answer, and then poll it. That is the only way to watch a poll miss, because in real life the truth arrives after the poll and nobody can go back.

The truth we will use is the real one. In 2024, of everyone who voted for one of the two major candidates:

  • Trump 50.75%
  • Harris 49.25%

A margin of 1.5 points. Remember that number; everything today is measured against it.

Everything is base R. Work in order.

Part 1: A country we can see all of

truth <- 0.4925                      # Harris share of the two-party vote
N     <- 1000000                     # a million voters

population <- c(rep("Harris", round(N * truth)),
                rep("Trump",  N - round(N * truth)))

table(population)
#> population
#> Harris  Trump 
#> 492500 507500
round(100 * mean(population == "Harris"), 2)
#> [1] 49.25

We know the answer. No pollster ever does. That is the only thing that is unrealistic here, and it is the point.

Part 2: One poll

poll <- sample(population, 1000)
table(poll)
#> poll
#> Harris  Trump 
#>    485    515
round(100 * mean(poll == "Harris"), 2)
#> [1] 48.5

Not exactly 49.25, but close. Run it again and you get a different answer:

for (i in 1:3) {
  p <- sample(population, 1000)
  cat("poll", i, ":", round(100 * mean(p == "Harris"), 2), "\n")
}
#> poll 1 : 50.3 
#> poll 2 : 47.8 
#> poll 3 : 46.9

That wobble is sampling error — the only kind of error the ±3 describes.

Part 3: What the margin of error actually promises

Run a thousand polls and look at the spread.

estimates <- replicate(1000, 100 * mean(sample(population, 1000) == "Harris"))

hist(estimates, breaks = 30, col = "#BBBBBB", border = "white",
     xlab = "Poll estimate of Harris's share (%)", ylab = "Polls",
     main = "One thousand honest polls of 1,000 people each")
abline(v = 100 * truth, lwd = 3, col = "#B2182B")

moe <- 1.96 * sqrt(0.25 / 1000) * 100
c(margin_of_error = round(moe, 2),
  within_moe = round(100 * mean(abs(estimates - 100*truth) <= moe), 1))
#> margin_of_error      within_moe 
#>             3.1            94.5

The margin of error is ±3.1 points, and about 95% of the polls land inside it. The promise is kept exactly.

But read the promise carefully. It says: if my only problem is that I asked 1,000 people instead of all of them, I will usually be within 3 points. It says nothing whatever about any other problem.

Part 4: More people, less error

n <- seq(200, 20000, by = 100)
plot(n, 1.96 * sqrt(0.25 / n) * 100, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, col = "#54278F",
     xlab = "People polled", ylab = "Margin of error (points)",
     main = "Bigger polls are more precise")
abline(h = 3, lty = 3, col = "grey50")

for (k in c(500, 1000, 5000, 100000)) {
  cat(sprintf("n = %6d   margin of error = %.2f points\n",
              k, 1.96 * sqrt(0.25 / k) * 100))
}
#> n =    500   margin of error = 4.38 points
#> n =   1000   margin of error = 3.10 points
#> n =   5000   margin of error = 1.39 points
#> n = 100000   margin of error = 0.31 points

Familiar, and true. Now we break it.

Part 5: The problem that is not sample size

Everything above assumed that when you call somebody, they answer. In 2024 the response rate to a typical telephone poll was under 1%.

That would be survivable if the 1% who answer were a random 1%. They are not. Suppose Harris voters are somewhat likelier to pick up the phone — 20% likelier.

answers <- ifelse(population == "Harris", 1.20, 1.00)   # who picks up

biased <- sample(population, 1000, prob = answers, replace = TRUE)
round(100 * mean(biased == "Harris"), 2)
#> [1] 55.1

That is not sampling noise. Do it a thousand times:

biased_est <- replicate(1000,
  100 * mean(sample(population, 1000, prob = answers, replace = TRUE) == "Harris"))

hist(biased_est, breaks = 30, col = "#F4A58255", border = "white",
     xlim = c(45, 60),
     xlab = "Poll estimate of Harris's share (%)", ylab = "Polls",
     main = "One thousand polls, when Harris voters answer more often")
abline(v = 100 * truth, lwd = 3, col = "#B2182B")
abline(v = mean(biased_est), lwd = 3, lty = 2, col = "#2166AC")
legend("topright", c("the truth", "average poll"), col = c("#B2182B","#2166AC"),
       lwd = 3, lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")

c(truth = 100 * truth,
  average_poll = round(mean(biased_est), 2),
  bias = round(mean(biased_est) - 100 * truth, 2))
#>        truth average_poll         bias 
#>        49.25        53.88         4.63

The polls are still tightly clustered. They are just clustered around the wrong number. Averaging them together — which is what a polling average does — does not help at all, because they are all wrong in the same direction.

Part 6: The bit that should worry you

Bias does not care how many people you ask.

for (k in c(1000, 10000, 100000)) {
  s <- sample(population, k, prob = answers, replace = TRUE)
  est <- 100 * mean(s == "Harris")
  cat(sprintf("n = %6d   estimate %.2f   reported +/- %.2f   actually wrong by %+.2f\n",
              k, est, 1.96 * sqrt(0.25/k) * 100, est - 100 * truth))
}
#> n =   1000   estimate 57.70   reported +/- 3.10   actually wrong by +8.45
#> n =  10000   estimate 53.77   reported +/- 0.98   actually wrong by +4.52
#> n = 100000   estimate 53.69   reported +/- 0.31   actually wrong by +4.44

Look at the last line. A poll of 100,000 people reports a margin of error of ±0.31 and is wrong by about 4.5 points — roughly fifteen times its own stated precision.

And it does not drift toward the truth as \(n\) grows. It converges — on 53.8%, which is not the answer. More data makes you more confident about the wrong number.

This is the argument in Bailey’s Polling at a Crossroads, and it is why the polling industry’s problem in the last three presidential elections has not been one that a bigger sample could fix.

Part 7: Weighting, and why it is not a cure

Pollsters know this, and they correct for it. If you know Harris voters are over-represented, you can count their answers for less. The catch is that you have to know which variable is doing the damage, and be able to see it.

# A population with two attributes: how you vote, and something else about you
# — call it trust in institutions — that we will let drive who responds.
N2 <- 200000
harris <- rbinom(N2, 1, truth)
trust  <- rbinom(N2, 1, ifelse(harris == 1, 0.75, 0.45))
true_share <- 100 * mean(harris)

responds <- ifelse(trust == 1, 1.00, 0.35)   # low-trust people rarely answer
i <- sample(N2, 5000, prob = responds, replace = TRUE)
s <- data.frame(harris = harris[i], trust = trust[i])

round(c(truth = true_share, raw_poll = 100 * mean(s$harris)), 2)
#>    truth raw_poll 
#>    49.31    57.24

Weight on trust — the thing actually driving non-response:

target <- mean(trust)                            # the true share, if you knew it
w <- ifelse(s$trust == 1, target / mean(s$trust),
                          (1 - target) / (1 - mean(s$trust)))
round(c(weighted = 100 * weighted.mean(s$harris, w),
        error    = 100 * weighted.mean(s$harris, w) - true_share), 2)
#> weighted    error 
#>    50.48     1.17

Now weight on something real, measurable, and unrelated to who answers:

irrelevant <- rbinom(nrow(s), 1, 0.5)
w2 <- ifelse(irrelevant == 1, 0.5 / mean(irrelevant), 0.5 / (1 - mean(irrelevant)))
round(c(weighted = 100 * weighted.mean(s$harris, w2),
        error    = 100 * weighted.mean(s$harris, w2) - true_share), 2)
#> weighted    error 
#>    57.25     7.94

Weighting on the right variable takes the error from about +5.5 points to under one. Weighting on the wrong variable changes nothing — the estimate does not move.

So weighting works, exactly and only when you already know what is wrong. In 2016 the industry discovered it had not been weighting by education, and fixed it. In 2020 it missed again, in the same direction. The variable you have not thought of is invisible by construction, and no amount of arithmetic finds it.

Part 8: What to carry into Tuesday

A margin of error is a statement about sample size and nothing else. It is honest and it is narrow. It does not cover bias, and bias is the thing that has been going wrong.

Polling averages do not fix a shared error. If every poll is wrong in the same direction, so is the average of them.

And the errors have been correlated across states. When the polls miss, they tend to miss the same way everywhere at once, which is why the states you care about most are the ones where being wrong matters most.

On Thursday next week we will have the answers, and you can check the forecast you read against what actually happened.

Part 9: On your own

This is the part you turn in. You are not being asked to write code. Each option is a working chunk with one thing to change.

Pick one.

Option A — How big does the bias have to be?

gap <- 0.20                # <- change this. Try 0.05, 0.10, 0.40.

ans <- ifelse(population == "Harris", 1 + gap, 1)
est <- replicate(300, 100 * mean(sample(population, 1000, prob = ans,
                                        replace = TRUE) == "Harris"))

hist(est, breaks = 25, col = "#F4A58255", border = "white", xlim = c(44, 62),
     xlab = "Poll estimate (%)", ylab = "Polls",
     main = paste0("Harris voters ", round(100*gap), "% likelier to respond"))
abline(v = 100 * truth, lwd = 3, col = "#B2182B")

c(response_gap = gap, average_poll = round(mean(est), 2),
  bias = round(mean(est) - 100 * truth, 2),
  moe_claimed = 3.1)
#> response_gap average_poll         bias  moe_claimed 
#>         0.20        53.92         4.67         3.10

Write about: how small a response gap does it take to matter? Start at 0.05 — a 5% difference in willingness to answer, which sounds like nothing — and report the bias it produces. Compare that to the ±3.1 the poll would advertise. Then say what this implies for reading a poll that shows a 1.5-point race, which is what 2024 actually was.

Option B — Does averaging help?

n_polls <- 20              # <- change this. Try 5, 20, 200.

ans <- ifelse(population == "Harris", 1.20, 1)

honest <- replicate(n_polls, 100 * mean(sample(population, 1000) == "Harris"))
skewed <- replicate(n_polls, 100 * mean(sample(population, 1000, prob = ans,
                                               replace = TRUE) == "Harris"))

round(c(truth          = 100 * truth,
        avg_of_honest  = mean(honest),
        avg_of_skewed  = mean(skewed),
        spread_honest  = sd(honest),
        spread_skewed  = sd(skewed)), 2)
#>         truth avg_of_honest avg_of_skewed spread_honest spread_skewed 
#>         49.25         49.31         54.11          1.44          2.00

Write about: averaging many honest polls works — the average closes in on the truth as you add more. Averaging many biased polls does not, however many you add. Report both. Then the question that matters this week: polling aggregators average dozens of polls and report a very tight interval. What is that interval actually measuring, and what would have to be true for it to mean what readers take it to mean?

Option C — Weighting on the wrong thing

strength <- 0.35           # <- how strongly trust drives response. Try 0.1, 0.35, 0.8.

resp <- ifelse(trust == 1, 1.00, strength)
j <- sample(N2, 5000, prob = resp, replace = TRUE)
ss <- data.frame(harris = harris[j], trust = trust[j])

tgt <- mean(trust)
wr <- ifelse(ss$trust == 1, tgt/mean(ss$trust), (1-tgt)/(1-mean(ss$trust)))

round(c(truth       = true_share,
        raw         = 100 * mean(ss$harris),
        weighted    = 100 * weighted.mean(ss$harris, wr),
        raw_error   = 100 * mean(ss$harris) - true_share,
        wtd_error   = 100 * weighted.mean(ss$harris, wr) - true_share), 2)
#>     truth       raw  weighted raw_error wtd_error 
#>     49.31     55.90     50.06      6.59      0.75

Write about: as strength falls toward 1, non-response stops mattering and the raw poll is fine. As it falls toward 0.1, almost nobody low-trust answers and the raw poll is badly wrong — but weighting still rescues it, because we can see the variable. State plainly what would happen if the variable driving non-response were something the pollster does not measure. Then connect it to Week 9: attention and response are both behaviours we can observe, and belief is not.

Option D — Ask your own question

Change the truth to a landslide instead of a 1.5-point race and see whether bias still matters. Or find out how large a poll would have to be for its margin of error to shrink below the bias — a trick question worth answering.

What to submit. Knit to HTML or PDF and upload to Canvas, with your chosen chunk and two or three paragraphs of interpretation.

The writing is the assignment. I am not grading your code — it is my code. I am grading whether you can read a number with a ± after it and say what that symbol does and does not cover.

Where the data came from

Mostly, it did not. This lab is a simulation, and that is the design rather than a compromise: you cannot watch a poll fail unless you know the true answer, and with real polling data you never do until afterwards.

The truth the simulation is built around is real — the 2024 national two-party vote, Trump 50.75% to Harris 49.25%, from the compilation used in Week 4. data/pres2024_states.csv is the state-level file from Weeks 1, 2 and 6, copied here so the lab stands alone and so Option D can use it.

Two honest limits on what a simulation can show:

  • The response gaps here are invented. Twenty percent is a plausible-looking number, not a measured one. The shape of the argument is what transfers, not the size of any particular bias.
  • Real non-response is not one variable. It is many, correlated, and shifting between elections. Part 7 uses a single tidy variable so the mechanism is visible; reality gives pollsters no such favour.

If you want the real thing, the Cooperative Election Study (https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/X11EP6) publishes tens of thousands of interviews per cycle with its weights attached, and its documentation of how those weights were built is worth reading alongside Bailey.
